<process id="digital-typology" version="1.2">
    <title>Digital Typology</title>
    <purpose>
        Define and construct a definitive system graph by topologically converging the functional elements of an under-examination artifact into load-bearing parent types that structurally contain their specific, active operational roles within the joins, generated by recursing each Vested Entity's objective purpose for a join-specific encounter function received through the functionalities of each of its Providing Elements—ensuring the resulting joins express the atomic, active-voice realities particular to this specific artifact rather than its generic functional type.
        </purpose>
    <target type="path" value="/home/rich/metaform/src/metaform/modules/mcp" note="Location of the artifact to examine, name of the artifact in the working folder, or delivered outside of this structure as instructions in this message such as the critical structure of a system to be used as a functional mapping tool. Switch type to inline and put the artifact's content in value instead if there's no location or a latent space construction task." />
    <core_concepts>
        <concept term="AUE" full="Artifact Under Examination" definition="The entity (thing or things) being examined, created, or used. Artifacts can include photographs, contracts, stories, resale assets, and software. The work can concern multiple artifacts and projects. Whether an AUE serves as an asset depends on its use in that context." />
        <concept term="Join" definition="A dictionary object that exists in the Receiving Entity (RE) with a relation in active voice, an observation of the long lasting stable state of what is there; additionally it contains a dictionary of objects containing type specific or AUE specific references and logic." />
        <concept term="Element" definition="An element is any nameable part of an entity as a type; however, just because an element can be named doesn't mean it is interesting, remarkable, or deserving of special attention. Many elements can be immediately seen, or are easily inferred." />
        <concept term="Entity" definition='An entity is a whole, independent thing with its own distinct existence, while an element is a smaller part or component that makes up that whole. All entities are elements, but not all elements are entities. Entity or an element depends entirely on your level of abstraction (your scope). The moment you zoom into a component and examine its internal composition, that component transitions conceptually from a passive "element" into an active "entity" with its own subordinate elements.' />
        <concept term="OP" full="Operative Purpose" definition="The **why**. This is the active goal held in a Vested Entity's join dictionary — that an element's encounter function intends to accomplish." />
        <concept term="EF" full="Encounter Function" definition="The **how** of what is delivered.  This may be understood as the function of an encounter or the encounter of a function depending on the contextual understanding of the Artifact. This is the mechanism, interface, relationship, or method through which an AUE or Element performs its purpose for its Vested Entity. It explains how the effect is encountered, used, or experienced. The EF belongs to the Providing Element, but is stored in the Vested Entity-owned join because a PE element type's functionality on the whole may satisfy different Vested Entities' Operative Purposes through different Encounter Functions. Record the PE's EF for that specific encounter in the join; do not create a single element-level EF record outside its joins." />
        <concept term="RE" full="Receiving Element/Entity" definition="The **who** or **what** bearing an OP. This is the element, person, group, system, component, or other participant with an Operative Purpose for the Encounter Function of an Element. The OP belongs to that receiver, and the join that records it lives in that receiver." />
        <concept term="VE" full="Vested Entity" definition="The RE vested in the type of thing the artifact is: the type or party that holds an objective purpose for this type of object and drives the most improvement in it. The VE receives the join, holding the Operative Purpose that a Providing Element's Encounter Function serves." />
        <concept term="PE" full="Providing Element" definition="The part satisfying the requirement actively declared by its Vested Entity through its Operative Purpose. This is the join's other endpoint: whatever's EF fulfills the VE's OP." />
        <concept term="AT" full="Artifact Type" definition="This is a general category or classification that groups individual artifacts together based on shared characteristics. Artifact Types can be used to anneal or combine many of the same type of AUE into types (for example photos, data objects, scripts, templates, etc)." />
        <concept term="NE" full="Notable Element" definition="A component, interface, or specification that defines an essential demand or requirement. It is **notable** because it highlights what a system or component explicitly expects, needs, or depends on from its external environment to operate successfully." />
        <concept term="DE" full="Defining Element" definition="The notable element of this AUE whose loss would prevent the AUE from remaining the same type. Its Encounter Function services the OP of a VE outside of this AUE, names the functional type of the AUE as a converged result of the functionality of the AUE being examined. Its defining function is expressed independently of medium, encoding, genre, and style." />
        <concept term="SE" full="Substantial Element" definition="An element whose Encounter Function helps the DE serve the VE's OP. It counts as substantial because of what it is meant to contribute to this AUE, even when that contribution is subversive, weak, replaceable, or should be improved." />
        <concept term="Parametric" definition="A quality or quantity that can be tuned but does not carry a specific name in the scope of the namespace of this AUE. We do not name parametrics with a namespace address in this graph or as part of this operation." />
        <concept term="NS" full="Namespace Scope" definition="The scope of the Artifact Type. The five base valid types are code, document, media, data, and stakeholder." />
    </core_concepts>
    <vested_entity_rules>
        <rules>
            <rule>We call an entity outside the artifact vested because all we can do is infer its purpose.</rule>
            <rule>Assume an artifact is converted into a metaform to improve it. The VEs that matter are the ones whose purpose drives changes or improvements to the artifact. Enumerate each of them.</rule>
            <rule>The VE that drives the most improvement gives the best inference.</rule>
            <rule>Never the person who asked for the intake, and never the end user.</rule>
            <rule>The VE is the party vested in the type of thing the artifact is.</rule>
            <rule>The VE is especially important because it forms the tripartite join that makes each join artifact specific: the VE as receiver, its Operative Purpose as the why, and the Providing Element's Encounter Function as the how.</rule>
            <rule>Elements are types, so the VE is a type: the type of party that holds an objective purpose for this type of object, named at its most specific reusable type level.</rule>
            <rule>When one person can hold several roles, name the role that changes the artifact, by the title that role carries.</rule>
            <rule>Identify the VE by asking who drives the most improvement in an artifact of this type.</rule>
            <rule>Deciding on the VE takes deep consideration because it is not a present element in what you are examining. Infer it from what the artifact is; do not look for it in the artifact.</rule>
            <rule>The VE is not the developer, the user, or anyone performing the operation. That could be said of every artifact, so it identifies nothing about this one, and it is the wrong way to be reasoning.</rule>
        </rules>
        <examples type="vested_entity">
            <example artifact_type="media.photo" ve="seller" valid="true" reason="the seller goes out of its way to present the photo in the best possible way to facilitate a sale." />
            <example artifact_type="media.photo" ve="operator" valid="false" reason="the party performing the operation could be named for every artifact, so it identifies nothing about this one." />
            <example artifact_type="code.[not a programming tool]" ve="developer" valid="false" reason="Never state the user or the developer sitting on the other side of the screen; it's not the answer we are looking for, because it doesn't present unique reasoning. Pretend you are analyzing the artifact itself. Unless the type is code.ide or an actual programming tool, don't answer developer." />
            <example artifact_type="*" ve="End User" valid="false" reason="This is a non answer, it says nothing worthwhile to reason about." />
            <example artifact_type="document.story" ve="Reader" valid="true" reason="The reader is true because they are vested in reading a good story; they will be spending their time to read the story, and they want it to be good. Vested does not always mean money." />
            <example artifact_type="media.photo" ve="buyer" valid="false" reason="the buyer judges the photo; judging does not change or improve it" />
            <example artifact_type="media.photo" ve="insurance company" valid="false" reason="the insurance company records the photo and does not want it changed" />
            <example artifact_type="media.photo" ve="social media poster" valid="true" reason="a social media post drives changes or improvements to the photo" />
            <example artifact_type="media.photo" ve="blogger" valid="true" reason="a blogger drives changes or improvements to the photo" />
        </examples>
    </vested_entity_rules>
    <join_types>
        <join_type name="purpose" scope="intake" />
    </join_types>
    <namespace_rules>
        <rules>
            <rule>For each dotted part, the address in the namespace must be reversible and read as its name.</rule>
            <rule>All artifacts are entities, all entities are not artifacts, all entities are elements, all elements are not entities.  (Artifacts ⊂ Entities ⊂ Elements)</rule>
            <rule>Namespace entries must describe the type of functional approach as a proper noun.</rule>
            <rule>To be placed into the namespace, an entry must be the same thing as its parent type, or a function within its parent type, and never a non-functionality.</rule>
            <rule>There must be one or more entities each with a distinct unique objective purpose and encounter function for the defining element.</rule>
            <rule>Children must take their parent's name as their last name when reversed and read as a noun.</rule>
            <rule>Multi-word names: when the new leaf is a variant functionality of its parent type, such as physics engine and game engine, express the namespace with periods between the segments: code.engine.game, code.engine.physics. Every prefix is a complete type that yields its own inference and passes its practices to its children, so words that form a valid prefix of their own must remain separate segments. Words may be joined with underscores in one segment only when none of them forms a valid prefix, as in code.queue.dead_letter and data.bill_of_materials, where the name must also read correctly once reversed.</rule>
            <rule>Specify the name_length value indicating the lookback segment count as its acceptable short name that is well understood.</rule>
            <rule>The segments in the namespace can be reversed by replacing periods with spaces to read properly as an inferenceable, well understood name.</rule>
            <rule>It must be a part or type of its parent scope.</rule>
            <rule>Namespace must narrow from trunk to leaf.</rule>
            <rule>The namespace address names the type. The join refines that type with what this AUE does, so the address stays general and the join stays specific.</rule>
        </rules>

    <method deliverable_format="recorded with the intake tools">
        <steps>
            <step n="1" text="FOR each AUE; organize into AT groups capable of generating a useful imperative for an agent based on the (OP of the VE) and the (EF of the PE) of the AUE's DE in service of the VE's OP as the stakeholder; NEXT AUE. Where the intake receives a folder or collection, survey every member before grouping is finalized: observe each member, reason its AT, its DE, its SE and NE elements, and the OP and EF relationships that distinguish its functionality; group only members whose shared functionality supports the same AT-level imperative, while retaining member identity through refs where needed." />
            <step n="2" text="FOR each AT; create a namespace entry for the RE as a VE, add its OP and EF from step 1 in a join, and identify the members in that join's refs using key='path' and value='[relative path]'; NEXT AT." />
            <step n="3" text="FOR each AUE; FOR each AT; observe DE as a VE and decompose its requirements and dependencies as EF of other elements. The DE simultaneously remains the PE serving the external VE's OP where that relationship exists. Whenever an encountered element itself bears an OP, trace it as a VE without creating a duplicate namespace record. NEXT AT; NEXT AUE." />
            <step n="4" text="For each element with an EF that serves the intent of an OP, create a join record in the VE of type purpose; add the active OP statement as the purpose, the non_goal where the VE holds one, the Providing Element's Encounter Function as function, with ef set to Function if it is the encounter of a functionality or Encounter if it is the functionality of the encounter, the Providing Element's namespace address in the provider field, the relation as an active-voice descriptive fragment starting directly with a third-person singular present-tense verb ending in -s or -es, whose subject is the Providing Element when ef is Function and the Vested Entity when ef is Encounter, that verb as verb, high value observations consisting of long lasting stable state that describes this join, optional non-goals consisting of structural constraints, and refs where needed. Record each element and join as soon as it is reasoned, one object at a time, rather than holding the map until the end." />
            <step n="5" text="Perform this task recursively, starting with the element named in the first OP: move to the next element and treat it as the VE where it bears requirements or an OP of its own." />
            <step n="6" text="Find that element's OPs: what it needs and wants from the rest of the AUE, or from outside it, in order to deliver its own EF. Element functionality serves the OP of entities, so every OP found traces back through its receivers to the OP of the external VE." />

events.instructions:
Metaform keeps this project's functional map: what each part is for, who receives what it does, and how. Read the part you are about to change before you change it, so you work from its purpose. Each tool is a module of Metaform. Call a tool with no command to see its commands and what each takes; then call it with command, and the command's arguments in arguments. On the command line the same command is metaform <module> <command>. An error ends with the one next step to take.

If you cannot continue, stop and submit a trouble report: call the metaform tool with command feedback, attaching what you have in its shape field. Do not retry.

This project has a map. Before you change a part, call the map tool with command where and the part's address: it returns what the part is for, what relies on it and what it relies on. With no address, use command roots. Give work to an agent through Metaform: record the task at each element it concerns with command work, and hand the agent those addresses; the agent takes a task with op take and ends it with op done. When you need an answer from the user, ask at the part it concerns with command ask, in plain words and with the answers you suggest; then carry on with what does not wait on it.

Metaform keeps this project's functional map: what each part is for, who receives what it does, and how. Read the part you are about to change before you change it, so you work from its purpose. Each tool is a module of Metaform. Call a tool with no command to see its commands and what each takes; then call it with command, and the command's arguments in arguments. On the command line the same command is metaform <module> <command>. An error ends with the one next step to take.

If you cannot continue, stop and submit a trouble report: call the metaform tool with command feedback, attaching what you have in its shape field. Do not retry.

This project has a map. Before you change a part, call the map tool with command where and the part's address: it returns what the part is for, what relies on it and what it relies on. With no address, use command roots. Give work to an agent through Metaform: record the task at each element it concerns with command work, and hand the agent those addresses; the agent takes a task with op take and ends it with op done. When you need an answer from the user, ask at the part it concerns with command ask, in plain words and with the answers you suggest; then carry on with what does not wait on it.
